newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines again raises rates, stocks tumble.
newsitem.headline: Philippines again raises rates, stocks tumble.

text.p: The Philippines on Thursday raised interest rates again to defend the peso from speculators but appeared helpless to prevent a peso- linked fresh slump in its stock market.
The Philippine Central Bank raised its key overnight borrowing rate by two percentage points to 32 percent, its highest in 2-1/2 years.
At 0330 GMT, the peso was at 26.4 to the dollar, unchanged from its previous close.
The overnight rate has roughly doubled in the past week as the Central Bank tries to spare the peso the fate of Thailand's currency.
The Thai government last week responded to intense speculation against the baht by floating the currency in what amounted to a de facto devaluation.
But economists warned that high Philippine interest rates aimed at keeping the peso steady and inflation low could start to bite into economic growth.
"Raising interest rates will eventually have its cost," said Ces Tanchoco, economist of Bank of the Philippine Islands.

The stock market went into a freefall triggered by the peso uncertainty and fears that high interest rates will negatively impact some firms. At the opening, the index dropped more than four percent, the sharpest fall in three months. It later recovered some of the lost ground.
At 0335 GMT, the main index was at 2526.26 points, down 2.43 percent.
But some analysts said the end result of the currency chaos may be positive if it forces a depreciation of the peso, thus making the country's exports more competitive.
Though the Central Bank insists the peso's value is determined by the market, its recent aggressive intervention has ensured its level against the dollar has barely moved in close to two years.
"It's part of the transition to a more competitive economy. We'll end up with continued growth," said Jose Mario Cuyegkeng, research director of ING Barings Securities.
He noted that the Philippines went through the same pressures in 1993, when exporters had also urged a depreciation.
The peso eventually fell by 10.4 percent to an end-1993 level of 27.70 pesos, which helped gross domestic product post 4.4 percent growth in 1994 compared with two percent in 1993, Cuyegkeng said.
"We're entering this situation stronger," he said.
"When things settle down, the policy choice open for the Central Bank is to allow for a crawling depreciation of the peso... to maintain our competitiveness in the world market," added Tanchoco.
